title: Enterprise Adoption Velocity & Pricing Sensitivity: empirical research and action plan
creator: Asha Kapoor
description: Run a focused research sprint to quantify how enterprise customers trade off latency, per-token cost, and model feature surface when evaluating Redwood vs competing hosted and self-hosted inference options. Deliver empirical elasticities (pricing sensitivity) and a recommended set of tactical product/pricing experiments for H1.
background: Sales and Solutions Engineering have reported recurring objections: (1) model latency at scale, (2) model pricing vs alternatives (hosted API per-token vs reserved capacity), and (3) availability of specific model features (e.g., tool calling, structured output, multi-turn state persistence). We lack a consolidated, data-driven view of which dimension most strongly influences purchase velocity and commitment size for enterprise customers.
goals: 1) Estimate relative importance (weight) of latency, unit cost, and feature set in purchase decisions for 50+ enterprise accounts. 2) Produce elasticities: e.g., % change in conversion/commit given a 10% price reduction or 15ms latency improvement. 3) Recommend three prioritized product/pricing experiments and an impact estimate for each.
scope_out_of_scope: In scope: interviews, controlled pricing signaling tests on sales motions, analysis of usage/engagement funnels, competitive public pricing benchmarking, and small internal latency A/B tests on Dedicated. Out of scope: large-scale pricing redesign, legal contract changes, or infra capacity purchases—those will be follow-ups if experiments validate ROI.
research_plan: Weeks 1-2: stakeholder interviews (sales, solutions, support), collect contract/commit size history, and synthesize public pricing and feature matrices for top 8 competitors. Weeks 3-4: run controlled experiments: (a) price signaling variants in outbound demos (two variants), (b) targeted latency improvement demo for 8 high-intent prospects. Weeks 5: analyze results, draft recommendations and experiments for product/ops.
data_sources: CRM opportunity history (HubSpot) — closed/won vs lost reasons
Public competitor pricing pages and docs
Internal perf dashboards: runtime latency percentiles per model
initial_findings: Early sample (n=12) from interviews shows feature coverage > price for regulated verticals (finance, healthcare)
Mid-market accounts are highly price-sensitive; small price changes materially affect committed GPU pools
Latency concerns surface most strongly for real-time products (search, agent orchestration) vs batch embeddings
Competitor X bundles low-cost quantized models but lacks strong caching/rollout tools—customers trade off quality for cost in low-stakes workloads
competitive_implications: If pricing is the dominant lever for mid-market, we should prioritize a low-cost model tier combined with explicit quality SLAs and console cost-analytics. If latency dominates for high-value enterprise, invest in latency SLAs and latency-led collateral (benchmarks + SLO guarantees) rather than broad price cuts.
tradeoffs_considered: Offer deep price discounts vs increase friction by adding reserved capacity requirements
Improve latency by changing kernel scheduling vs invest in smarter routing and edge placement
Expose lower-quality quantized models to cut price vs risk of regression in evals
decisions: Run two micro-experiments in Q1: price signaling in 40 outbound demos (Variant A: -10% list; Variant B: -20% for 6-month commit) and latency-centric demo for 10 high-intent prospects.
Focus initial low-cost model tier on mid-market use cases (search, summaries, simple extraction) with clear documentation on expected quality differences.
